title: Sherpa Runtime Quirk Notes and Microfix Prototypes
body:
Purpose:
A lightweight synth of recurring customer threads about unexpected runtime behaviour (mostly around KV cache and batching edgecases), plus a short list of microfix prototypes engineering can spike this sprint. Name is intentionally silly — think of this as the Sherpa guide: small, local fixes that reduce friction for customers while we scope proper engineering work.

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- Several mid-market customers report intermittent latency spikes when conversations exceed ~3k tokens; symptoms: sudden 200–400ms tail spikes per-token during generation, higher memory churn, occasional OOMs on Dedicated nodes.
- Common trigger: rapid alternating short/long requests from same session, leading to inefficient KV cache eviction and re-warm.
- Workaround currently used by CS: force shorter max_length or restart session — both poor UX.
- Short-term microfixes likely to help: smarter soft-eviction heuristics, lightweight prefix-store on host, and a quick flag to disable continuous batching per-client for spikey sessions.

Evidence / customer threads (anecdotal):
- Customer A (fintech): intermittent 350ms tail latency during chat summarization, noticed correlation with long (>2.5k) back-and-forth sessions. Logged to JIRA-1234.
- Customer B (marketplace): saw OOMs on Dedicated pool when combining embeddings and generation in same session; workaround created: separate endpoint for embeddings.
- Customer C (enterprise legal): complains that session resets are disruptive to users and hurt evaluation metrics.

Quick reproducer steps (dev note):
1) Start session with model redwood/gemini-small (seq_len 4096) on Dedicated dev node.
2) Send alternating messages: 3x short (10 tokens), 1x long (2.8k tokens), repeat 6 times.
3) Observe per-token latency via tracing: watch for sudden jumps and KV cache re-fill traffic.
4) Capture heap profile at spike.

Observed traces / metrics pointers:
- Token throughput dips while kernel context-switches increase (perf counters), suggesting cache misses.
- KV cache fill traffic shows repeated cold read patterns for recently-evicted keys.
- Tail-latency percentiles: p95 stable, p99 shows spikes.

Microfix candidates (priority order for spikes to lowest risk):
A) Soft-eviction bias: avoid evicting keys for sessions that have >50% short-requests in last N minutes. Implementation: add session recency+size score and prefer evicting the largest contiguous ranges first. Quick test: feature-flagged on a single rack. (JIRA-1278)
  - Risk: slightly higher memory use; mitigations: TTL for 'protected' keys.
B) Session-prefetcher (cheap): on detection of long request following short bursts, prefetch likely KV pages asynchronously so generation doesn't block. Prototype: thread-pool spike that reads predicted indices. Low code change; can be A/B toggled per-customer.
  - Risk: extra IO, but can be gated by a budget counter.
C) Per-client continuous-batching disable flag (expose as routing policy): if a client shows oscillating seq-length distribution, run them with batching disabled for X minutes. Simple to implement in router layer.
  - Risk: CPU inefficiency; offset by run only on affected sessions.
D) Minimal user-visible session-restart endpoint: offer customers an API that gracefully checkpoints and reinitializes a session without losing context (server provides small tokenized snapshot). This reduces CS manual guidance to restart sessions.

Prototype plan for A and B (two-week spike):
- Week 1: implement soft-eviction heuristic behind feature flag in runtime (Ravi + Jon). Add telemetry counters for hits/misses and memory delta.
- Week 1: implement async prefetcher prototype (Emilia) with budget guard; run on dev rack.
- Week 2: run canary with two willing customers (Customer A & C) under a short trial; collect p50/p95/p99 and memory usage.
- Success criteria: reduce p99 spikes by >=40% during reproduced scenario without >10% increase in average memory.

Customer-facing language (for CS template):
- "We're piloting a small runtime improvement that reduces unexpected latency when a conversation mixes very short and very long messages. If you'd like to opt in to a test we can enable it for your Dedicated capacity and monitor impact. It won't change your model outputs and can be toggled off any time."

Engineering asks (specific):
- Add feature-flag scaffolding in runtime for 'soft-eviction-protect' per-session. Attach metrics: protected_key_count, prefetch_hits, eviction_count_by_strategy. (Owner: Ravi)
- Small router toggle to mark session as "batching-protected" when seq-length oscillation threshold passed. (Owner: Jon)
- Quick perf harness: script that runs reproducer with configurable short/long ratios and reports p99/p999 latencies and memory. (Owner: Emilia)

Risks & unknowns:
- Interplay with quantized models and kernel selection — prefetching could be less useful for some quant paths. Need research note.
- Some Dedicated customers maintain strict memory budgets; any protection that increases memory needs opt-in.
- A/B noise: p99 improvements may vary across instance types; must run across at least two hardware families.

Open questions for product/ops:
- Should microfix be opt-in per-customer (safer) or default-on for hosted tier (riskier but broader benefit)?
- Is there a privacy/regulatory concern with checkpointing session snapshots for graceful restarts? (Legal)

Next steps / sprint commitments:
- CS: reach out to Customer A & C for pilot opt-in (Ava) by 2025-10-07.
- Eng: spike A/B prototype for soft-eviction + prefetch on dev rack by 2025-09-25 (Ravi/Emilia).
- Product: decision on default vs opt-in by 2025-10-01.
- Ops: reserve a canary Dedicated slot and enable extended traces for pilot (Jon).

Notes-to-self / informal:
- Keep Sherpa label internal (cute but not external-facing).
- Consider adding a simple telemetry dashboard tile under Console: "session-oscillation events" so CS can triage quickly.
- If spike root cause turns out to be kernel-level thrash, escalate to infra kernel team — this doc will track that handoff.

Appendix: quick trace excerpt (annotated):
- t=0: short request, p50=7ms
- t=1: short request, p50=6ms
- t=2: long request, p50 jumps to 12ms, p99 spike to 380ms, KV refill indicated
- t=3: short request, p50 returns but p99 remains elevated until eviction TTL expires

End of notes.

-- Ava M.
